item.title: What are you holding when you hold gold?
item.description:
After its peak at $5,318 per ounce in January, gold price has dipped to about $4,000 right now, marking a drawdown of about 25%. Because gold is non-yielding (i.e. holding it does not generate any interest), the opportunity cost of holding gold is the interest a saver could earn by lending to the government. Given recent increase in yield on 10-year Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (10Y TIPS), which is a Treasury bond whose principal adjusts to inflation and rise in energy price, the drop in gold price seems reasonable. Yet, when we zoom out a little, the price of gold has actually doubled since 2021, while the 10Y TIPS rate rose 3.6 percentage points. This seems to contradict the theory that there is an inverse relationship between gold and the real interest rate.

Other factors seem to dominate the movement, at least periodically. Usually, there are three candidates other than real interest rate: dollar, stocks, and oil. I regress gold’s weekly return on all four at once, so each number below is one factor’s effect with the other three held fixed. This post tries to answer: which of these exposures does the price of gold carry, how big is each, and does that change after 2022? Understanding the correlations and movements can be important to central banks, especially those in the emerging market, as they divert away from U.S. government bonds and dollars when Russian accounts were frozen. Knowing which risk gold actually carries is also pertinent to anyone who wishes to invest in assets with relatively stable long-term return, since gold is a precious physical good with inherent value and no credit risk.

Gold’s exposure to dollar, real yield, stock, and oil

The interactive figure below gives a rolling sensitivity analysis of gold against other factors, with a two-standard-error confidence band. Click the dropdown menu to select the factor/asset.

  • Dollar. Over the past twenty years, for every 1% increase in dollar index, gold price drops by 1.6% on average. The exposure remains negative and has barely exceeded 0 even for the upper bound of the interval. There is a very clear and persistent negative link between dollar and gold.
  • Real yield.A one-point rise in the 10-year real yield lowers gold by 3.5% with the dollar held fixed. Real yields and the dollar usually rise together, though. If we count the stronger dollar that comes with real yield, a one-point rise has gone with a 6.3% fall in gold. The link between real yield and gold is rather unstable as the two-year estimate swings from -14 to +6.
  • Stock. Before 2022, a 1% fall in the S&P 500 came with a 0.2% rise in gold, making gold a weak hedge. Since 2022, the estimate is zero. This makes sense as commodities have historically exhibited low correlation with equities.
  • Oil. The direct exposure of gold to oil is close to zero in every window. Yet, energy price shock affect gold price indirectly through real yields and dollar. Before 2026 oil did not move real yields, but in 2026 an oil jump pushed real yields and the dollar up, and gold fell about 1% for every 10% rise in Brent.
  • Drift. There is also the return none of the four factors explains, which is about 11% a year before 2022 and 21% since. Figure 3 will return to it.

Figure 1. Two-year rolling regression of gold’s weekly return on the four factors

Is gold still a safe asset?

Figure 2 plots gold’s monthly total returns against three types of portfolio. The rust dots are the the worst 10% of months for a portfolio, and the blue dots are the rest of the months. When we hover over the dots, we can see the return for both in each month. The dropdown menu allows us to select each portfolio. For the portfolio with 60% stock ETF and 40% Treasuries, the average return in the worse 10% of the month is -4.4%. In those months gold averaged -0.9% and rose 48% of the time, below its usual 55%. If we switch the dropdown to pure S&P500 ETF, before 2022 gold rose in 76% of the worst equity months, and since 2022 in only 2 of 8 (too few sample to draw any conclusion yet). Finally, for the pure bond portfolio, gold fell 2.9% on average in the worse Treasury months. The rate exposure from Figure 1 is showing up exactly when bonds lose money.

Figure 2. Monthly total returns from month-end prices, February 2003 to October 2026

Where the returns actually came from

Figure 3 decomposes the contribution of each of the factors to gold’s yearly return. The colored pieces are what the four exposures account for, and grey is the unexplained factor. We could hover over the bars to see the detailed decomposition. Clicking a legend entry can remove a component and allows us to see what remains.

In the past five years, the unexplained factor accounts for a significant proportion of gold’s return. In 2024 and 2025, the grey bar is about twice the size of any year before 2022.In 2022, real yields and dollar both rose, and they together contributed to -17 log points to gold’s return. However, gold price ended flat because the the drift added +13 points, offsetting the downward pressure from higher yields and stronger dollar.

More strikingly, in 2024, gold rose 27% against the backdrop of stronger dollar, and +44 log points was due to the unexplained factor. 2025 continued the trend, with the drift contributing 55 points.

Figure 3. Each factor’s contribution is its full-sample coefficient x the factor’s cumulative move that year, in log points so the pieces add up to the year’s return

What might the drift be?

Prices cannot say what the drift is, but there are two candidates. Central banks bought more than 1,000 tonnes of gold a year in 2022-24, over twice their 2010-21 average of 473;1 a buyer who ignores TIPS yields and the dollar shows up here as pure drift. But their buying slowed to 863 tonnes in 2025, the year the drift peaked, while gold ETFs took in 801 tonnes.2 So central banks fit 2022-24, and investors fit 2025 better. Both remain hypotheses.

Takeaway

Holding gold is first a bet against the dollar (1.6% per 1%, steady for twenty years) and second a bet against real yields (6.3% per point, half of it through the dollar). Oil enters only through those two, and there is not direct link between oil and gold. Gold cannot be insurance for a 60/40 portfolio because it rose in 48% of the worst months and falls when bonds fall. And since 2024 these exposures explain none of its rise in gold. The 120% came from a drift that prices alone cannot explain, and that turned negative in 2026.

Data and code

Gold: COMEX gold futures, front-month continuous contract (GC=F), daily close in US dollars per troy ounce; stocks: SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY); bonds: iShares 7–10 Year Treasury ETF (IEF), both dividend-adjusted — all from Yahoo Finance via yfinance. Real yield: 10-year Treasury inflation-indexed constant-maturity yield (DFII10, Federal Reserve Board H.15); dollar: nominal broad trade-weighted dollar index (DTWEXBGS, Federal Reserve Board); oil: Brent crude spot (DCOILBRENTEU, EIA) — all from FRED. Daily data from 2 January 2003 (the dollar index from 2 January 2006, where the four-factor regressions start) to 22 October 2026; accessed 24–25 October 2026. Regressions use weekly (Friday-to-Friday) changes with Newey–West standard errors; the hedge test uses monthly total returns from month-end prices; the 60/40 portfolio is 60% SPY and 40% IEF, rebalanced monthly.

Code, data and every number quoted above: github.com/1iiiiii/Gold-vs.-Real-Yield.

Footnotes

  1. World Gold Council, Gold Demand Trends: Full Year 2024, central banks section: 2024 was the third consecutive year above 1,000 tonnes, against an annual average of 473 tonnes in 2010-2021. https://www.gold.org/goldhub/research/gold-demand-trends/gold-demand-trends-full-year-2024/19411↩︎

  2. World Gold Council, Gold Demand Trends: Full Year 2025, central banks section (net purchases 863 tonnes; 2024 revised to 1,092 tonnes) https://gold.org/goldhub/research/gold-demand-trends/gold-demand-trends-full-year-2025/central-banks; ETF inflows of 801 tonnes as reported in “Gold demand tops 5,000 tonnes for the first time”, Graphic Online, 1 February 2026.↩︎

item.title: Matching parents and children with SQL
item.description:
If your parents earned twice what a neighbor’s parents earned, how much more will you earn compared to the neighbor’s children? This questions is the motivation for the Great Gatsby curve and the “American Dream” debate. Policy economists comparing countries and people arguing about whether the US is a land of opportunity both reach for the same number (the intergenerational elasticity (IGE)) to answer it.

Most of the debate is about how big that number is. This post asks a prior question: how much of a parent’s income advantage reaches the children, and does the answer depend on when income is measured? It does. Measuring a parent’s income in a single year, or a child’s income too early in their career, makes the US look more mobile than it is. In the data used here, a single year of the father’s income hides about 40% of the persistence. This post walks through the whole pipeline, from raw survey file to estimation using SQL inside Python, so a reader with basic Python and SQL can redo it.

What the intergenerational elasticity measures

Intergenerational elasticity (IGE) measures the link between parents’ income and their children’s income after they leave the family. The equation is:

It is a log-log regression of child income on parent income, where β is the IGE. A β of 0.4 means that if one father earned 10% more than another, his children earn 4% more than the other’s children on average. A β of 0 means there is no relationship, and a β of 1 would mean a caste system where there is no mobility whatsoever.

Introduction of the data source

The Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID) began in 1968 has interviewed the same people, their children, and their grandchildren. It interviewed them every year until 1997 and every two years since, most recently in 2023. Because children are followed when they leave home, the same file contains a father’s income in 1985 and his daughter’s income in 2015. That is what makes a parent–child match possible.

We rely on two unique identifiers for the match.

  • Every person’s permanent ID. This is the interview number of the family they were first observed in 1968 (for the original families) plus a person number within it. It never changes.
  • Interview number each family gets every year. Income is recorded once per family per year under that number, and each member’s record carries the same number. So a person’s record says “in 1990 I was in family 517”, and the family record says “family 517 earned $38,400 in 1989”.

The raw data downloaded from the Data Center gives one wide spreadsheet , and the first job is to turn it into three tables. A table with individuals, a table with one row per person-year and a table with one row per family-year can be joined on (year, interview number). A wide file cannot be joined this way, because each year’s values sit in a different column. All incomes are converted to 2023 dollars with the Consumer Price Index (CPI), so a dollar in 1975 and a dollar in 2015 buy the same amount.

Table One row per Rows Key
individuals person 85,536 permanent ID (id_1968, person_num)
persons person × survey year 910,869 permanent ID + year; interview, age and relationship to head
families family × survey year 320,456 year, fam_interview; total family income (adjusted based on 2023 CPI)

Step 1: Filter the children

A child observation is a person-year in which the person becomes the head of their own household or is the spouse of the head, aged 25–45. The relationship filter is needed and we can’t rely on age alone. For example, a 32-year-old still living with their parents carries the parents’ income on their record.

SELECT id_1968, person_num, year, age, interview
FROM persons
WHERE rel_head IN (1, 2, 10, 20, 22)   -- head or spouse; the codes changed in 1983
  AND age BETWEEN 25 AND 45;

SELECT picks columns, FROM chooses the table, and WHERE filters those rows we need. Note that there is code change in 1983, so 1 and 2 are before 1983 and 10, 20, and 22 are after. Refer to the codebook for more information. We should get 259,398 persons-years from 34,533 people.

Step 2: Attach each person-year to its family’s income

The JOIN clause lines up rows of two tables that share a key. The key here is (year, interview number). We should check the row count before and after JOIN. Same count means nothing was duplicated and every person-year found its family.

SELECT p.id_1968, p.person_num, p.year, p.age, f.fam_income_real
FROM persons AS p
JOIN families AS f
  ON p.year = f.year AND p.interview = f.fam_interview
WHERE p.rel_head IN (1, 2, 10, 20, 22)
  AND p.age BETWEEN 25 AND 45;

We use INNER JOIN here because we want to drop a person-year with no family record. That is, the family is not interviewed during that year.

Step 3: JOIN on identifiers to find each child’s father

The individuals table has the child’s own ID in two columns and the father’s ID in two other columns. Joining the table to itself, the child’s father columns against the father’s own ID columns, is the parent–child match.

SELECT c.id_1968, c.person_num,
       dad.id_1968, dad.person_num
FROM individuals AS c
LEFT JOIN individuals AS dad
  ON c.father_id_1968 = dad.id_1968
 AND c.father_person_num = dad.person_num;

A LEFT JOIN here keeps every child and fills the father columns with NULL when no match exists, so the NULLs can be counted. Of 34,533 people in the child sample, 24,690 have no father in the data. Among the 24,690 NULLs, 15,316 was because their parents were never surveyed, and 9,374 was because the father’s ID points to someone not in the extract. The matched children we get are those whose fathers were PSID members.

We then join the father’s ID to his rows in persons, and those to families, keeping the years when the child was 13–17. The reason we use a window between 13-17 is that it measures the family’s resources while the child was growing up. About 70% of the children in the final sample were born by 1980, so they turned 17 before the survey became every two years.

SELECT c.id_1968, c.person_num,
       fp.year, fp.year - b.birth_year AS child_age,
       f.fam_income_real
FROM individuals AS c
JOIN birth    AS b  ON b.id_1968 = c.id_1968 AND b.person_num = c.person_num
JOIN persons  AS fp ON fp.id_1968 = c.father_id_1968
                   AND fp.person_num = c.father_person_num
JOIN families AS f  ON f.year = fp.year AND f.fam_interview = fp.interview
WHERE fp.year - b.birth_year BETWEEN 13 AND 17;

Here birth is a small helper table with each person’s birth year, computed from their age in each survey year.

Step 4: Comparing one year of income with several years

After JOINing, we then aggregate the data to get the income information we want. GROUP BY collapses many rows per child into one, and we are grouping by two identifiers, and the two together identify one person. AVG takes the mean and COUNT gives the number of rows. We build two parent income measures. The first is the single year when the child was closest to 15, and the second is the average over the observed years at ages 13–17. We require at least two observed years, so both measures use the same 3,951 children. That way, any gap between the two estimates comes from how income is measured, not from comparing different families.

SELECT id_1968, person_num,
       AVG(fam_income_real) AS parent_inc_avg,
       COUNT(*)             AS parent_years
FROM father_income
GROUP BY id_1968, person_num;

Result 1: One year of parent income understates the IGE

Each dot is the average child income among about 200 children whose fathers had similar incomes, and the lines are regression fits. Both axes are on a log scale, so each line’s slope is β. Gold uses the father’s income in the single year the child was about 15, and blue uses the same fathers’ average over the child’s ages 13 to 17.

Averaging raises the IGE from 0.25 to 0.43 for the same children, so the single-year measure understates it by about 40%. A single year’s income is long-run income plus that year’s luck, such as a bonus or a layoff, and the luck flattens the line toward zero. Averaging cancels much of it (Solon 1992).

Result 2: Age when the children’s income is measured

Each point is the same regression, with parent income averaged over the child’s ages 13 to 17 but the child’s income measured in a single year at the age on the horizontal axis. The band is the 95% confidence interval, and the dashed line is the estimate from Result 1, which averages the child’s income over ages 30 to 40.

The IGE rises from 0.25 at age 25 to 0.52 at 40, then falls to 0.45 at 45. At 25, many children of high-income parents are still in school or early in steep careers, so their income that year understates their lifetime income more than it does for other children (Haider and Solon 2006). Fewer children are observed at older ages (3,753 at 25, 1,881 at 45), so part of the pattern may reflect who is in each group.

Takeaway

In the PSID, a father’s income averaged over his child’s teenage years gives an IGE of 0.43. A father who earned 10% more than another has children who earn about 4.3% more in their 30s. The two results show two different problems, and both push the estimate down. A single year of the father’s income mixes long-run income with temporary luck, which averaging fixes (0.25 rather than 0.43). A child’s income at 25 understates their lifetime income, which measuring near mid-career fixes (0.25 at 25 rather than 0.52 at 40). A multi-year average is the better measure of long-run economic status because the temporary ups and downs cancel while the persistent level stays. Finally, to answer the opening question. If your parents earned twice as much as your neighbor’s, you would expect to earn about 35% more than the neighbor’s children (20.43 ≈ 1.35), not the 19% (20.25 ≈ 1.19) that a single-year measure suggests.

Data and code

Source What Access
Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID), public-use data, 1968–2023 Individual file: permanent person ID, sex, father’s and mother’s IDs, and per wave age, interview number, relationship to head, sequence number. Family files: family interview number and total family money income PSID Data Center custom extract
U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, CPI-U all items (CPIAUCSL), via FRED Annual-average CPI used to express all incomes in 2023 dollars (PSID income in survey year t refers to calendar year t − 1) FRED CSV endpoint, accessed 23 October 2026

Code, the SQL, and every number in this post: github.com/1iiiiii/Intergenerational-Mobility.

References

  • Haider, S. and G. Solon (2006). “Life-Cycle Variation in the Association between Current and Lifetime Earnings.” American Economic Review 96(4): 1308–1320.
  • Solon, G. (1992). “Intergenerational Income Mobility in the United States.” American Economic Review 82(3): 393–408.

item.title: Home prices outran incomes in most of the country since the pandemic
item.description:
In post 4, we investigated the drivers of increasing mortgage rates, and in this post, we are delving into the other pillar of housing affordability: housing price. High mortgage rates are a national story, but housing prices vary significantly from county to county. As such, using county-level data would give us a more granular perspective of the trend of housing prices that a national median/average hides.

Looking at home prices alone wouldn’t give us a concrete sense of how affordability has been changing, so we will be using price-to-income ratio. The ratio is the median home value divided by median household income. It is a yardstick for how expensive homes are relative to what people earn. The ratio has increased from 2.9 to 3.5 in the past decade in the typical county with at least 50,000 people, showing a persistent rise in home prices relative to household income.

Rising home prices make it particularly harder for first-time buyers who are saving a down payment, since the amount of down payment is in proportion to housing prices. This would also affect employees who are deciding whether to relocate to where their jobs are. It would then be important for those potential homebuyers to take geography into consideration when deciding whether and where to purchase a house. This blog post asks: where did home prices pull furthest ahead of incomes between the late 2010s and the early 2020s, and what do those places have in common?

How to measure home price relative to income?

  1. Taken at face value, the price-to-income ratio tells us the number of years it would take for a median household income to pay for the entirety of the house, which is unrealistic. Therefore, the level of the ratio itself matters less than how the ratio moves. This ratio would be the baseline for how we measure the changes, and dividing dollars by dollars from the same survey year cancels inflation.

  2. We would also be looking at the percent change between two five-year windows, 2015-19 and 2020-24. A 17% rise means prices grew about 17% faster than incomes: in the typical county, home values rose 48% and incomes 27%, and 1.48 ÷ 1.27 ≈ 1.17. Percent change is better at reflecting the underlying trend. For example, the same 10% relative rise would add 0.7 to a ratio of 7 but only 0.2 to a ratio of 2, so a level change would make places that are already expensive look worse just because they started high. Another benefit of looking at a change rather than the ratio itself is that the ratio only shows where homes are expensive, while the change shows where affordability got worse.

  3. Counties are the finest unit with a reliable median for the whole country. The map shows all 3,095 continental counties with data, and the comparisons below use the 990 counties with at least 50,000 people, where the survey’s estimates are steadier.

Where prices pulled ahead

On an aggregated level, the price-to-income ratio rose in 87% of the counties on the map, with only 403 of 3,095 counties seeing a fall in the ratio. More strikingly, 96% of people in the mapped counties live in a county where it rose. A cluster of counties in the interior West (Idaho, Utah, Nevada, Montana), central and east Texas, Tennessee, Georgia, and Florida, have seen ratios rise by more than 30% (deepest red on the map). Coastal California and much of the Northeast pale in comparison to the deepest reds because while homes there are expensive, their prices are not outpacing incomes by a significant amount.

Several counties have extreme rises in the ratio. For example, in Clayton County, Georgia, in the southern suburbs of Atlanta, home values rose 105%, whereas incomes only rose by 25%, so the ratio increased by 64%. Less extreme rises are Twin Falls (+59%) and Bonneville (+56%) in Idaho, and Hunt County (+50%) in the Dallas exurbs of Texas, but they still far outpaced the typical county’s 17%. It is noteworthy that every one of these counties started cheap, with ratios of 2.2 to 3.2, near or below the typical larger county’s 2.9.

Nonetheless, there are exceptions. Manhattan’s ratio actually fell by 8%, and in counties whose population mostly shrank or grew slowly, such as in the rural Southwest, Louisiana and the Ohio valley, incomes grew faster than home values. What these places share is that people were not moving in.

What explains the rise

Each grey dot is a county with at least 50,000 people, and each red dot is the average of about 50 counties with similar population growth. In counties whose population shrank by about 5%, the ratio rose 11%. The fastest-growing twentieth averaged about 20% growth, and the ratio rose 30%, nearly three times as much.

One likely reason is that during and after the pandemic, people moved toward cheaper, roomier, warmer places, and housing there could not be built fast enough, so newcomers bid prices up faster than local incomes rose.

Could it be that places that were already expensive simply pulled further ahead? The data say no. A county’s starting ratio is, if anything, slightly negatively related to how much its ratio rose (a correlation of −0.12), while population growth is clearly positively related (0.46). Cheaper places caught up, and where people moved, not where prices already were, predicts the rise. Had we measured the change in the ratio’s level instead of in percent, the starting ratio would have looked positively related (+0.26), purely because high ratios move more in absolute terms.

Caveats

  • The analysis only reveals the pattern rather than the causes of rising home prices. While growth and rising prices move together, other factors like climate or cheaper starting prices could drive changes in both.
  • The Census home value is what owners estimate their home is worth, not a sale price, and it covers owner-occupied homes only, while household income covers all households, renters included.
  • Each window is a five-year average, so the 2021-22 price spike is blended in, not shown at its peak.
  • A county is not a housing market, and a big county can hide a hot town next to a cold one. Small rural counties are also noisy in the survey, which is why the map looks speckled in the Plains and why the comparisons use counties of 50,000+.

Takeaway

Since the late 2010s home prices outran incomes in most of the country: by about 17% in the typical larger county, and by 50% or more in fast-growing suburbs and small cities of the South and the interior West. The places people moved to saw their price-to-income ratios rise about three times as much as places that people moved out from, and it was growth, not already-high prices, that predicted the rise. This suggests that affordability likely hinges on whether fast-growing places can build, not only on mortgage rates.

Data and code

Source What Access
U.S. Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates, 2015–19 and 2020–24 County median home value (B25077), median household income (B19013), population (B01003); 2020–24 also workers and work-from-home (B08006) Census API, /data/2019/acs/acs5 and /data/2024/acs/acs5, accessed 16 October 2026
U.S. Census Bureau, cartographic boundary files, 2024 County polygons at 1:500,000 (cb_2024_us_county_500k) Downloaded from census.gov, accessed 16 October 2026

item.title: Expectation of real interest rates and inflation expectations are driving up the bond yields and mortgage rates
item.description:
The 30-Year Fixed Mortgage Rate is the most common type of U.S. home loan. As its name suggests, it takes borrowers 30 years to pay back the entire loan, and the interest rate is fixed at the then-current mortgage rate when the contract is signed. The mortgage rate has risen from 2.74% in January 2021 to 6.86% in September 2026. By the time this blog post is written, the national average is approximately 7.40% to 7.43%.1

The causes of the high level of mortgage rate are intricate, as they involve several layers of transmission, each layer represents stakeholders that are pertinent to the rates. The chain starts with the Federal Funds Rate. The Fed raises this rate in order to curb inflation, and the housing market is the main channel of monetary policy. The Fed cares about indirectly managing mortgages through raising the federal funds rate. This ultra short-term rate then directly affects the yields on 10-year Treasury, which is the benchmark of mortgage rates. Higher mortgage rates means home purchases are less affordable, and this matters to all potential homebuyers. According to Atlanta Fed, the median monthly payment of home purchase takes about 27.8% of a median household income in January 2021. Now it takes more than 45%, effectively deterring many buyers.2

The blog post tries to address two questions: how much of the rise is the Treasury yield, how much is the spread, and within the Treasury yield, is it expected real rates, expected inflation, or risk premia?

Two decompositions

The benchmark for mortgage rate is the 10-year Treasury yield. That is, mortgage rate tends to closely follow the 10-year Treasury (as opposed to the Federal Funds rate). The difference between the 30-year mortgage rate and the 10-year Treasury consists of two spreads: (i) secondary spread: prepayment risk, credit risk, and liquidity, (ii) primary-secondary spread: service fee, net guarantee fee, etc. This post will treat the two spreads as a whole and the equation is simply . This is not only for simplicity, but more importantly, as we will discuss later in the post, the spread is not the main driver of the higher rates in the current period. Our focus is on the decomposition of the 10-year Treasury yield. The Cleveland Fed’s term-structure model breaks the 10-year Treasury yield into four components: expected path of real short rates, expected inflation, real risk premium, and inflation risk premium. The equation below gives a clearer representation of everything put together:

where:

  • : expected real interest rate (the average real short-term rate expected over the next ten years)
  • : expected inflation rate
  • : real risk premium
  • : inflation risk premium
  • : Cleveland Fed’s model residual (the gap between the actual 10-year yield and the model’s fitted yield)
  • : mortgage-Treasury spread

Three data choices follow. All series are converted to monthly averages, so that weekly, daily and monthly data line up on the same dates. January 2021 is the base month for every “change since” calculation, because that is when the mortgage rate bottomed; a trough base maximizes the measured change by construction. The model residual is kept as its own piece, so that the six pieces add up exactly to the change in the mortgage rate.

The spread’s history

Figure 1 gives a simple decomposition of the 30-year mortgage rate. The spread’s long-run norm is 1.69 pp on average from 2010 to 19, and it peaked at 2.97 pp in June 2023. It is now printing at 1.87 pp, which is just slightly above the long-run average pre-pandemic and post-GFC.

Decomposition and share of contribution

Figure 2 shows the complete decomposition of the mortgage rate. The blue bar indicates expected real short rates, which is the market’s expectation of future path of monetary policy. It has been the main driver of mortgage rates and 10-year Treasury for the majority of the sample period. We could see that even at the October 2023 peak, the spread was only a quarter of the story, and inflation expectation and expected real rates are predominantly leading.

To get a more concrete sense of what’s driving the changes in mortgage rates, we could look at the share of contribution by components in three different periods, shown in the table above. The period from January 2021 to October 2023 saw rates from trough to peak, the main driver being the market’s expectation of the short-term policy rate (41%). The spread comes next at 24%. But if we look at a longer window from January 2021 to September 2026, the contribution of mortgage-Treasury spread shrinks to 5%. What’s more pertinent to the scope of this blog post is the year-to-date contribution. Since the beginning of 2026 until now, expected real short rates and expected inflation together accounts for 97% of the increase in mortgage rates.

To put those numbers into context, several forces have been pushing on different pieces of the decomposition. Fiscal concerns, such as the rising debt-to-GDP ratio and higher interest payments, would show up as a higher real risk premium, but that piece explains only part of the story. Higher energy prices would show up in the inflation risk premium, which is almost negligible at 1%. Debt issuance related to AI investment is not necessarily reflected in the model. Resilient economic growth feeds through to expected inflation.

Cleveland Fed’s model vs. NY Fed’s model

The Cleveland Fed’s model is only one way of decomposing the rates, and it would be conducive to check it against other models, such as New York Fed’s ACM model along with Treaury Inflations-Protected Securities (TIPS). THe table below shows that both models agree that expected policy path, not the term premium, is the main driver, and in 2026 both say all of it. TIPS data also supports the same framing. Over Jan 2021 and Sep 2026, the TIPS real yield rose 3.64 pp and the breakeven 0.27 pp, suggesting that the market believes the rise was almost all real. However, the models disagree on the exact contribution of term premium. From January 2021 to September 2026, while the Cleveland Fed’s model indicates that term premium contributes 0.23pp, the NY Fed’s model claims it contributes 1.31 pp. It is noteworthy that Cleveland’s expected inflation rose more than breakevens. Its model had 10-year expected inflation at 1.38% in January 2021 against a 2.08% breakeven.

What moves the spread

Panel 1 shows that the spread spikes line up with the volatility spikes in 2008–09, spring 2020, and 2022–23. The mechanism is the prepayment option. A homeowner can refinance whenever rates fall, so the investor holding the mortgage is short that option. When rate volatility rises, the option is worth more and investors demand a wider spread to hold mortgages. Volatility went from about 50 bp in 2021 to about 145 bp in early 2023, and the spread from 1.4 pp to 2.97 pp. In Panel 2, the Fed’s balance sheet shows up in the spread too. The cleanest episode is 2009 wheb holdings go from zero to 1.1 trillion in about a year and the spread falls from 2.9 pp to 1.3 pp, even though volatility was still high. Since 2024, the Fed is still shrinking its holdings, yet the spread has come back to 1.87 pp, near its 2010–19 average. Volatility fell from ~140 bp to ~70 bp over the same period. So the recent normalization tracks volatility, not the Fed’s balance sheet, which suggests the prepayment-option channel is the stronger of the two.

Caveats

  • The components for the decomposition are model estimates (Haubrich–Pennacchi–Ritchken), and a different model splits them differently (see Table 2) and we could potentially arrive at different conclusions. But in this case, different models at least agree with each other about the main driver.
  • The model does not fit the 10-year yield exactly. The residual averages −0.33 pp over the sample and reaches 1.23 pp in absolute value, but it moved only 0.17 pp between January 2021 and September 2026, so it does not change the ranking of the pieces.
  • The base month is the trough of the mortgage rate, which maximizes the measured change by construction. A later base, such as the first Fed cut in September 2024, would give smaller numbers but the same ordering.
  • The spread is the Freddie Mac survey rate minus the 10-year constant-maturity yield. It is not an MBS option-adjusted spread, so it mixes the secondary-market spread with lender margins and fees.

Takeaway

To conclude, of the 4.13 pp rise in mortgage rates since January 2021, 3.91 is the Treasury yield and 0.22 is the spread. Within the Treasury yield, the expected path of real policy rates accounts for 2.31 pp (56% of the mortgage move) and expected inflation for 1.19.

Risk premia are small under the Cleveland model and about a third of the Treasury move under the NY Fed’s ACM model. The spread problem of 2023 has largely gone, but the rate problem has not.

Data and code

  • Mortgage rate: Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey, 30-year fixed, via FRED (MORTGAGE30US), weekly. All FRED series were downloaded with fredapi on 4 October 2026.
  • Treasury yields: Federal Reserve Board H.15, via FRED: 10-year constant maturity (DGS10), 10-year TIPS (DFII10), 10-year breakeven (T10YIE), daily.
  • Fed MBS holdings: Federal Reserve Board H.4.1, via FRED (WSHOMCB), weekly.
  • Yield decomposition: Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland, Inflation Expectations, via FRED: EXPINF10YR, REAINTRATREARAT10Y, TENEXPCHAREARISPRE, TENEXPCHAINFRISPRE, monthly.
  • Term premium cross-check: Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Treasury Term Premia (Adrian, Crump and Moench), daily file, downloaded 3 October 2026.
  • Affordability: Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta, Home Ownership Affordability Monitor.
  • Code: github.com/1iiiiii/Mortgage-Rate-Decomposition. Four numbered notebooks download the data, build the monthly series and contributions, and save the figures and every number quoted above to results/.

Footnotes

  1. Freddie Mac’s Primary Mortgage Market Survey, which is the series used throughout this post, averaged 7.28% for the week of 1 October 2026 (7.03% the week before). Freddie Mac, 1 October 2026.↩︎

  2. Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta, Home Ownership Affordability Monitor: the share of median household income needed to cover the payment on a median-priced home, with 30% as the affordability threshold.↩︎

item.title: Decomposition of Differences between CES and CPS Employment Data
item.description:
The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) publishes two monthly measures of U.S. employment. The payroll survey, also known as the Current Employment Statistics (CES), asks businesses how many jobs they have and produces the nonfarm payroll number from my first post. The household survey, also known as the Current Population Survey (CPS), asks households whether their members are working.

A problem that the payroll number is facing is that it has become harder to read. The CES response rate hovered around 60% in the decade before the pandemic and has since fallen below 45%,1 which makes its early estimates less reliable. As such, analysts, markets and the Fed increasingly check it against the household survey. But the two don’t usually agree. In 2025 the household survey found about 163.5 million employed people, while payrolls counted about 158.4 million jobs, which is a gap of 5.1 million. Before one survey can check the other, we need to know what that gap is made of. This post asks how much of it is simply the two surveys counting different things, and how much is left over, or the residual.

Comparison between CPS and CES

Household survey (CPS) Payroll survey (CES)
Counts people with a job jobs
Sample about 60,000 households about 119,000 businesses and agencies
A person with multiple jobs counted once counted multiple times
Self-employed, unpaid family, private-household workers counted not counted
Farm workers counted not counted
On unpaid leave counted as employed not counted

The unincorporated self-employed run their own business that is not a corporation, such as a freelance designer. Unpaid family workers work without pay in a relative’s business, and private-household workers, such as nannies, are employed directly by a household.

BLS publishes a recipe, which I will call the bridge, for translating one concept into the other. Starting from household employment (), I subtract the groups payrolls exclude: agriculture (), the unincorporated self-employed (), unpaid family workers () and private-household workers (). Then I add back the second jobs of multiple jobholders (). Whatever still separates the result from payroll jobs () is the residual ():

The five bridge terms are definitional differences, each estimated from the CPS microdata. The residual is what the definitions cannot explain, so it is where at least one survey is off.

Data and weights

The household data are IPUMS CPS basic monthly microdata from January 2019 to August 2026. October 2025 is missing because the survey was not collected during the government shutdown. IPUMS distributes the CPS as one record per person surveyed rather than as the totals BLS publishes, which lets me build each bridge category myself. Payroll jobs are total nonfarm employment in their latest revised version. Both series are not seasonally adjusted, meaning the regular swings within each year, such as holiday hiring, are left in. That is because the CPS microdata are unadjusted, and both sides have to be on the same basis.

Each respondent carries a weight, the number of people they stand in for: a weight of 2,000 means 2,000 people. I use COMPWT, the composite weight BLS uses for its published estimates. It reproduces BLS’s January 2019 employment total of 154.964 million exactly, while the basic weight WTFINL overshoots it by 616,000.

The gap

The top panel plots each survey’s monthly total before any bridging, and the bottom panel plots the gap between them. The household survey sits above payrolls in every month. The gap was about 7 million in 2019 and narrowed to between 2 and 4 million by late 2024. Both series are unadjusted, so the gap wobbles with the seasons, but the jump of about 4 million between December 2024 and January 2025 is too large to be seasonal. To see what drives a move like that, the gap has to be decomposed.

Decomposition by Year: CES vs. CPS

Each bar is the number of people in one bridge category, averaged over the year. They are measured against a baseline of zero gap, which is what we would see if the two surveys counted exactly the same thing. Bars above zero are groups only the household survey counts. The red bar is second jobs, which only payrolls count, so it pulls the household count back. The grey bar is the residual, and all the bars add up to the black dot. Years with an asterisk are incomplete, since 2025 lacks October due to government shutdown, and 2026 ends in August.

Definitional differences account for most of the gap in every year: 4.4 of the 6.6 million in 2019, and 3.6 of the 5.1 million in 2025. Self-employment is the largest single component, usually around 9 million. Second jobs grew from 7.7 million in 2019 to 8.4 million in 2025. Relative to 2019, that offsets 0.7 million more of the household survey’s extra workers, which accounts for most of the 0.8 million fall in the definitional part of the gap.

The grey residual is the more interesting part. It was 2.2 million in 2019, under 1 million from 2020 to 2023, negative in 2024, and back to 1.5 million in 2025. That swing follows from how the household survey is built. Its weights are scaled so the sample adds up to the Census Bureau’s estimate of the U.S. population, so a higher estimate raises every weighted count. Each January the survey switches to new population estimates and never revises earlier months. BLS reports that the January 2025 update added 2.0 million to employment relative to the old estimates, mostly because of higher estimated immigration. My microdata show the same in that household employment usually falls about 0.8 million from December to January, but in January 2025 it rose by 1.05 million, about 1.9 million more than a typical January.

The update can also move in the other direction. In January 2026, lower estimated net migration and a Census methodology change cut household employment by 1.4 million, according to BLS. My decomposition shows a shortfall of about 1.2 million against a typical January.

Residual Analysis

The solid line is the monthly residual. Above zero, the bridged household count exceeds payrolls, and below zero, it falls short. Both population updates show up as jumps at the dotted lines, and the break in late 2025 is the missing October. The dashed line is a possible explanation the bridge leaves out. Wage and salary workers who have a job but were absent from work in the survey week.

The residual’s largest move, though, is not in a January. Between February and April 2020 it fell by about 5 million, while absent wage and salary workers jumped from 3.5 million to 9.6 million. Unpaid absentees count as employed in the household survey but not on payrolls, so if they were driving the residual it should have risen. Instead it fell. One possibility is the payroll survey’s reference period. Payrolls count anyone paid for any part of the pay period that includes the 12th of the month, so workers laid off after the 12th still appear as jobs. Another is that in-person household interviews were suspended that spring, so the household survey was measuring less precisely just when the labor market moved fastest.

Takeaway

Most of the gap between the two jobs numbers is definitional. After removing self-employment and farm work (which only the household survey counts) and adding back second jobs (which only payrolls count), the two surveys agree to within about a million in most years. The household survey can therefore check payrolls, but only after bridging and only once the residual’s large moves are explained.

Those moves have identifiable causes. In 2024 the residual went negative, meaning the household survey sat too low relative to payrolls, and the January 2025 population update then raised household employment by about 1.9 million more than a typical January. So at least part of the household survey’s weakness in 2024 came from its population base, not from the labor market. In spring 2020 the residual also went negative, but there the likelier causes are the payroll survey’s pay-period definition and disrupted household interviews. The practical rule is to compare the two surveys only after bridging, and to treat a January jump in household employment as a population revision until shown otherwise.

Data and code

  • Household survey: IPUMS CPS basic monthly samples, extract cps_00003. Sarah Flood, Miriam King, Renae Rodgers, Steven Ruggles, J. Robert Warren, Daniel Backman, Etienne Breton, Grace Cooper, Julia A. Rivera Drew, Stephanie Richards, David Van Riper, and Kari C.W. Williams. IPUMS CPS: Version 13.0 [dataset]. Minneapolis, MN: IPUMS, 2025. https://doi.org/10.18128/D030.V13.0
  • Payroll survey: BLS Current Employment Statistics, total nonfarm, not seasonally adjusted, via FRED (PAYNSA), accessed 28 September 2026.
  • Bridge method: BLS, Employment from the CPS adjusted to the CES concept.
  • Population controls: BLS, January 2025 adjustments and January 2026 adjustments.
  • Code: github.com/1iiiiii/Data-Visualization-in-R.

Footnotes

  1. Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, Do Low Survey Response Rates Threaten Data Dependence?, Economic Letter, March 2025. https://www.frbsf.org/research-and-insights/publications/economic-letter/2025/03/do-low-survey-response-rates-threaten-data-dependence/↩︎

item.title: How Feasible is Sweetgreen’s Expansion Goal?
item.description:
Sweetgreen is an American fast-casual restaurant chain that specializes in healthy, made-to-order salads, grain bowls and protein plates. On 19 September 2026 its website listed 299 U.S. locations, 292 open and 7 coming soon. In 2022, its CEO said the company intended to reach 1,000 restaurants by the end of the decade.1

For a restaurant chain, revenue growth comes mostly from opening new stores, so a fundamental equity analyst covering Sweetgreen needs to know whether the store count built into the forecast is realistic. This post asks whether the 1,000 target needs adjusting and, setting the 2030 deadline aside, where the remaining ~700 restaurants could plausibly go.

To answer it, I scrape the store locations of Sweetgreen and Chipotle, match every store to its metro area, and compare where each chain has chosen to open. Chipotle serves as the control since it’s also a fast-casual chain, but it’s much further along with about 4,155 U.S. stores. It separates what matters for Sweetgreen specifically from what matters for restaurants in general. Because a single snapshot cannot tell a small market from a young one, I also recover Sweetgreen’s store lists from 2016 and 2018 through the Internet Archive and follow its first markets over time.

Data

Sweetgreen lists its entire store base on one server-rendered page, so a single request returns all 299 locations. Chipotle publishes a sitemap that encodes the state and city of each of its 4,155 stores, so two XML files cover all of them. There are two fixes needed to match stores to metro areas. First, some locations in cities like Boston loses the leading zero in the ZIP codes. For example, 02109 appeared as 2109, so we need to recover the correect codes. Second, we need to add New York’s boroughs and New England’s towns, which are not Census places. After both, 95.7% of Sweetgreen locations and 95.2% of Chipotle stores match a metro area, and the 280 open Sweetgreen stores in U.S. metros are the base for everything that follows.

Sweetgreen Opens in Educated Metros

If Sweetgreen could match Chipotle’s density of 13.3 stores per million residents everywhere, it would support about 3,800 restaurants. That assumes every metro suits Sweetgreen equally, so I first need to know what kind of metro Sweetgreen builds densely in. A regression measures how store density varies with each of a metro’s characteristics while holding the others fixed, and the fitted relationship can then be applied to metros with no stores yet.

For each chain separately, I regress log stores per million residents on log median household income, log population density and the share of adults with a bachelor’s degree. These are the questions store managers think about because they need to know whether residents can afford it, whether enough people live close together to support a store, and how many are college-educated. I use only the metros each chain has entered (47 for Sweetgreen, 353 for Chipotle), because a metro with no stores has a density of zero and the log of zero is undefined. Taking logs puts two chains of very different sizes on the same percentage scale, so each coefficient reads as a percentage change in store density.

Each dot is a metro, and each line is fitted to one chain. Because the vertical axis is on a log scale, the steeper Sweetgreen line means its density responds far more to how educated a metro is. A one-percentage-point rise in the bachelor’s share is associated with about 6.6% more Sweetgreen restaurants per capita, but only about 1.0% more Chipotles, and the two coefficients are roughly four standard errors apart. Income adds nothing once education is known. The two move together across Sweetgreen’s metros (correlation 0.55), and income’s coefficient is indistinguishable from zero once education is held fixed.

New Cities Add Only About 120 Stores

Carrying the fitted relationship to the 340 metros Sweetgreen has not entered gives about 120 more restaurants, for a total of about 400 (fitting in levels instead of logs gives 406). The largest opportunities are Portland (about 4 stores), St. Louis (3.5), Orlando (3.4), Pittsburgh (3.2), Kansas City (2.9) and Cincinnati (2.8). These metros are simply less educated. Their median bachelor’s share is 29.5%, against 40.6% in the metros Sweetgreen serves.

So new cities can supply about 120 of the remaining ~700 restaurants. The rest would have to come from the 47 metros Sweetgreen already operates in, raising them to about 880 restaurants, or 5.5 per million residents. That is 3.1 times their current 1.7, and denser than any large market Sweetgreen runs today.

Existing Markets Fill In Slowly

Each line follows one of the nine metros Sweetgreen had entered by January 2018. Solid segments connect the two archived store lists, while dashed segments jump to September 2026, because no list is provided in between. Population is held at its 2019–2023 level, so every rise is new stores. The grey dashed line is the 5.5 per million the target requires.

The six metros Sweetgreen was in by January 2016 now average 2.6 stores per million, against 1.1 for the 38 it entered after January 2018. Part of what makes a metro look sparse today is simply that Sweetgreen arrived recently, so the 400 above is best read as what the footprint supports at its current stage, not a permanent ceiling.

But even the oldest markets fill in slowly. Washington, where Sweetgreen started in 2007, went from 25 stores in January 2018 to 30 today. The six oldest metros together rose from 1.4 to 2.6 stores per million between January 2018 and September 2026, about 0.15 per million a year. At that pace they would need roughly another 20 years to reach 5.5.

Takeaway

The 1,000 target is not a bet on Sweetgreen finding new cities. It is a bet that its existing markets fill in far faster than its oldest ones ever have. Sweetgreen’s own filings point the same way: it opened 35 net new restaurants in 2025 and 25 in 2024.2 At 35 a year, the roughly 290 restaurants open today become about 440 by the end of 2030, and 1,000 arrives around 2046, the same twenty-year horizon the density trajectory gives. Reaching 1,000 by 2030 would take about 165 net openings a year from here, nearly five times the 2025 pace.

A revenue forecast should therefore use something close to 440 restaurants for 2030 as the base case and treat 1,000 as a long-run ceiling. Two numbers would justify moving the forecast up: annual net openings rising well above 35, and density in Washington and Boston continuing to climb past 5 per million, which would show that even mature markets have room left.

Caveats

  • Unobserved appeal that is only available to Sweetgreen Sweetgreen opens where it expects high local appeal I cannot observe, such as office density, lunch culture and rents. The metros it has not entered are probably weaker than their education levels alone suggest, so the 120 is more likely too high than too low.
  • A gap in the history. No archived store list survives between January 2018 and September 2026, so I cannot tell whether Washington’s growth stopped in 2019 or slowed gradually. The archived lists are also only as complete as the copies the Internet Archive happened to save.

Data and code

  • Sweetgreen locations: sweetgreen.com/locations, one request, 19 September 2026.
  • Chipotle locations: locations.chipotle.com/sitemap1.xml and sitemap2.xml, two requests, same date.
  • Metro population, income and education: American Community Survey 2019–2023 5-year estimates, via tidycensus.
  • Place, town and metro boundaries: Census TIGER/Line 2023, via tigris.
  • Archived Sweetgreen store lists: Internet Archive Wayback Machine copies of sweetgreen.com/locations from 13 January 2016 and 3 January 2018, fetched 24 October 2026.

Code: github.com/1iiiiii/Web-Scraping-in-R contains the scripts and cached raw responses

Footnotes

  1. Restaurant Dive, Sweetgreen on track for 1K units by 2030 despite profitability challenges, 11 August 2022. https://www.restaurantdive.com/news/sweetgreen-1000-restaurants-by-2030/629384/↩︎

  2. Sweetgreen, Inc., Form 10-K for fiscal year 2025, U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1477815/000162828026012520/sg-20251228.htm↩︎

item.title: How to interpret the initial print and revisions of the Nonfarm Payroll Data?
item.description:
Nonfarm payrolls (NFP) are a count of paid jobs at U.S. businesses and government agencies, excluding farming. The data are estimated by the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) from a monthly survey of employers. The Federal Reserve closely monitors this indicator to keep track of whether one of its dual mandate (i.e. maximum employment) is achieved, which in turn affects the economy as a whole and the financial market.

However, the sophisticated statistical methodology of the measure makes it rather hard to interpret beyond the headline. The number that markets reacts to is the initial print, but it is revised several times afterwards. Those revisions became front-page news in August 2025, when the July report revised May and June job downward by a combined 258,000, and the President called for the BLS commissioner to be fired the same day.1

Ever since the pandemic, the amount of each revision has been nontrivial. This post asks: how reliable the initial print is, and how a reader should interpret it? It explains where the number comes from and how it is revised, and then splits revisions into the part caused by new data and the part caused by re-estimating the seasonal adjustment.

I. What the number is

  • Definition: Nonfarm payroll employment counts paid employees on the payrolls of nonfarm establishments, a group that accounts for roughly 80% of the workers who contribute to U.S. GDP.2
  • Source & frequency: The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) collects the data from private businesses and government agencies on a monthly basis and usually publishes it on the first Friday of each month at 8:30 a.m. ET.
  • Reference period: A person counts as employed if they worked or received pay for any part of the pay period that includes the 12th day of the month.3
  • The measure excludes: “sole proprietors, the unincorporated self-employed, unpaid volunteer or family workers, farm workers, and domestic workers,” along with active-duty military personnel.4

II. How the number is obtained

Sources of data

There are two BLS programs that measure the same thing at different frequency, and the relationship between them explains most of what follows.

The Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) is assembled from the unemployment insurance tax reports that essentially every employer is required to file with its state. It is close to a census: in 2025 it covered 12.1 million establishments and 155.7 million employees.5 About 97% of nonfarm employment within the scope of the establishment survey is covered by UI, and therefore visible to BLS through QCEW records.6 The price of that completeness is speed. QCEW is quarterly, and each quarter is published within six months of the quarter’s end.7

The BLS also runs the Current Employment Statistics (CES) survey, which is a monthly sample drawn from that same UI-derived universe, covering about 119,000 businesses and government agencies and approximately 622,000 individual worksites, roughly 26% of all nonfarm payroll jobs.8 CES reports about three weeks after the reference period rather than six months after the quarter.

Below is a comparison table of the two surveys.

Source: BLS, Employment Situation Technical Note (August 2026); CES National Benchmark Article; Employment and Wages, Annual Averages 2025; QCEW Overview.

III. How the number changes

There are three structurally different operations that all get called a revision, yet they have different causes, sizes and meanings. The mix of terms makes the revisions very obscure, but this is easier to hold onto once we sort them by the data sources behind them. This post uses the terms in the first column throughout. The naming is based on my own interpretation of each data. The BLS names are the official ones, but they are harder to keep straight.

Source: BLS, CES Frequently Asked Questions.

The first three rows all rest on the CES sample. Each is built from whatever survey responses have arrived by the time of publication, which is exactly what “preliminary” means here. That is, the data are open to change as the rest of the sample reports. The last two rows rest on QCEW instead. That is why they arrive once a year rather than once a month, and why they reset the level of employment rather than nudging a single month’s change.

Two of the official labels can seem misleading, as there are two “finals”. The “final estimate” is final only in the sense that no further monthly revision is coming, but the benchmark still is. And the benchmark figure that makes the news is almost always the preliminary benchmark, which is itself revised by the “final benchmark” the following February.

The monthly cycle

CES “revises its initial monthly estimates twice, in the immediately succeeding 2 months, to incorporate additional sample receipts from respondents in the survey.”9 For example, the June NFP data has its initial print in early July. In early August, not only does BLS release the initial print of the July NFP data, but it also releases the first monthly revision of the June data, as well as the second monthly revision of the May data. In early September, when the August NFP is released, June receives its second monthly revision.

Source: BLS, Current Employment Statistics revision table.

The annual benchmark

The final benchmark is published with the initial print of January NFP in early February of the following year, and it affects 21 months of previously published data, anchored to March of the previous year.10

Source: BLS, CES Frequently Asked Questions; BofA Global Research, QCEW: 2025 FAQs, 3 September 2025.

The 12 months up to the March anchor get the QCEW revision, and the 9 months after it are only rescaled and re-modelled. BofA states that April–December 2025 payrolls “will not be revised based on the QCEW until 2027.”11 So a payroll number is roughly eighteen months old before anyone checks it against tax records.

Decomposition of Revisions

A revision is the difference between the latest published number for a month and its initial print. A month’s number can change for two reasons.

The first is new data. Some employers don’t answer to the survey on a timely manner, and BLS revises trhe number as new survey responses arrive. The second is seasonal adjustment. The headline number is seasonally adjusted, meaning BLS removes the hiring and layoffs that happen at the same time every year, so that what is left is the unusual part.

BLS also publishes the series without seasonal adjustment, and that version changes only when new data arrive. This lets me split every revision in two:

Here SA is the seasonally adjusted number and NSA the unadjusted one. The revision to the unadjusted number is the part due to new data, and whatever remains of the total revision is the part due to the re-estimation of the model.

Source: author’s calculations from ALFRED vintages. Total nonfarm, thousands.

Figure 3 does the same split for every month. The blue bar is the part due to new data, the orange bar the part due to seasonal adjustment, and the black line is their sum, which is the revision BLS actually published. Over the 47 months from September 2022 to July 2026, three things stand out.

  • Revisions have mostly been downward, and new data is the reason. The average month was revised down by 61,000. New data accounts for 50,000 of that and seasonal adjustment for 11,000, which is why most blue bars sit below zero.
  • Seasonal adjustment still moves the number a lot. Its ups and downs largely cancel out on average, but ignoring direction, the seasonal part averaged 48,000 a month, against 71,000 for new data. It was the larger of the two in 20 of the 47 months.
  • The two parts often offset each other. In 26 of the 47 months they moved in opposite directions, as in October 2024. When that happens, the published revision is smaller than the total change underneath it.

A Falling Response Rate

CES response and collection rates
Year Overall response rate Collected at 1st release Collected at final release
2016 60.8 74.7 95.7
2019 59.3 73.9 93.2
2022 45.2 65.4 94.0
2025 42.2 65.2 91.5
2026 43.3 63.0 —

Source: BLS Office of Survey Methods Research. Annual averages, percent.

One of the main drivers of the large revisions is due to a falling survey response rate from the employers. The overall response rate has fallen roughly 18 percentage points since 2016, yet the share of employment collected by final closing has barely moved. Both are true because collection is employment-weighted, and large employers still report. What the survey is losing is small establishments, which is the same population the birth-death model is extrapolating over.

Takeaway

To conclude, the initial print is an early estimate and not a final count. On average, the initial print overstated job growth in this period. Over the 47 months from September 2022 to July 2026, first prints were revised down by 61,000 on average, and 50,000 of that came from new data (late survey responses and the benchmark).

I would read the data from three angles. First, since a single month is noisy, we could look at the 3-month moving average. Three months is chosen because it combines the latest initial print with the two previous months, which are revised with late responses. We could then see if the current month has any anomalous movement against the average. Second, I would look at the size and direction of revision for each month in the past five years. As the decomposition above shows, the downward drift has come mostly from new data rather than seasonal adjustment, so it has been a consistent pattern rather than noise. That gives a rough sense of where the current print is likely to be revised, though not an exact number. Third, I would break the headline down by sector or industry. This shows what is driving the total, and lets me check those sectors against other sources.

Footnotes

  1. WTTW News, Trump Demands Official Overseeing Jobs Data Be Fired After Dismal Employment Report, 1 August 2025. https://news.wttw.com/2025/08/01/trump-demands-official-overseeing-jobs-data-be-fired-after-dismal-employment-report↩︎

  2. Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, All Employees, Total Nonfarm (PAYEMS). https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/payems↩︎

  3. BLS, CES Frequently Asked Questions. https://www.bls.gov/web/empsit/cesfaq.htm↩︎

  4. BLS, Handbook of Methods: Current Employment Statistics — Concepts. https://www.bls.gov/opub/hom/ces/concepts.htm↩︎

  5. BLS, Employment and Wages, Annual Averages 2025. https://www.bls.gov/cew/publications/employment-and-wages-annual-averages/current/↩︎

  6. BLS, CES National Benchmark Article. https://www.bls.gov/web/empsit/cesbmart.htm↩︎

  7. BLS, QCEW Overview. https://www.bls.gov/cew/overview.htm↩︎

  8. BLS, Employment Situation Technical Note, August 2026. https://www.bls.gov/news.release/empsit.tn.htm↩︎
